findings.description: FAIL, change 5 does not close. The instrument added to all four fixture tasks is a no-op on exactly the fixture shape those tasks are told to build. lint-scope.sh classifies every file in pass one and puts only `schema: 2` files into `v2_files`; a file with no `schema` key increments the v1 counter and hits `continue` (lint-scope.sh:421-424). Pass two iterates `v2_files` alone, and check_tokens, check_open_questions, check_tensions and check_contradictions are further gated on `! has_v1_body` (lint-scope.sh:435-448), so a `body_schema: 1` file skips them too. A v1 fixture is therefore linted for nothing but file shape, and `must exit 0` is guaranteed before the worker writes a line. I verified it: copying `old-only` and appending `[open-question: freeze-owner]`, `[tensions: unacknowledged]` and `[memory candidate: journal]` to one note, `bash inbox-to-memory/scripts/lint-scope.sh <copy>` printed `failures: 0` and exited 0. That last token is the specific trap T-006's own excerpt names ('`[memory candidate: journal]` is not a token and never was'), and it passed. The three check_methods each assert the opposite as the reason for running it: T-002 'a malformed token in this fixture is invisible to every other check here and silently disables the behavior the scenario grades', T-005 'A malformed `[open question: <slug>]` is invisible to the count and disables the behavior the scenario grades', T-006 'the instrument for C-7's signal is actually there'. The worker-facing text says it too, and says it as fact: T-002 'a token invented at the point of use is a lint failure', T-005 '`[open question: <slug>]` and `[tension: ...]` are both registered shapes ...; a malformed one is a lint failure'. All false for a v1 fixture. Worse, each of those same excerpts steers the worker to v1 one paragraph away — T-002 and T-005 both say 'v1 files (no `schema` key) are legal forever and the lint never flags them', and T-003 requires v1 outright ('Build the gradable notes as v1 — no `schema` key'), which makes the instrument provably vacuous there rather than merely likely to be. The failure this lets through is the one the constitution's opening names: a fixture whose `[open question: <slug>]` is misspelled passes lint, passes C-1, passes C-11, and the skill's recurrence grep at SKILL.md:115 never fires, so C-6's scenario grades nothing while every check in the decomposition is green. Three ways out, any of which works: require the token-bearing notes to carry `schema: 2` without `body_schema: 1` so the lint actually reads them; or replace the instrument with the skill's own greps run against the fixture (`grep -rhoE '\[open question( resolved)?: [^]]*\]' <fixture>/notes/` for T-005, the machine-contracts.md row greps for T-002 and T-006); or drop the claim and say plainly that on a v1 fixture lint-scope.sh checks file shape and nothing else, so token fidelity is checked by reading. What is not available is leaving the sentence as written, because it tells both the worker and the checker that a green exit settles a question it never asked.

findings.description: PASS, and this is the change that had to land. The self-contradiction is gone and nothing narrows. 'run each clause's `check` field from .agent-guild/state/constitution.md in full, exactly as written there. Nothing in this task narrows any of them, and no conjunct of any of them is satisfied by an upstream verdict. The clause text is the contract' is a complete instruction on its own, and it is the operative one: it precedes the upstream paragraph and governs it. On the specific worry — whether the 'not exhaustive' list reads as the set a checker should look for — it does not, for three reasons that hold together. The list is preceded by the universal that generates it ('Every conjunct of those clauses that binds the document to a fixture was therefore unreachable upstream and is reached for the first time here'), so a checker has the rule and not just its instances. It is explicitly flagged ('Concretely, and not exhaustively'). And it sits under a heading that frames the paragraph as orientation ('What upstream tasks did and did not settle') rather than as a checklist. The four instances are each real and each correctly derived: expected-token-to-input pairing is C-7's second conjunct, positive/negative row-to-slug pairing is C-6's, per-row decidability against the emitted extract is C-8's, and the `tests/fixtures/` run target is C-10's fourth. The closing line does the rest of the work — 'A well-built fixture and a document that grades it backwards both pass upstream; only this check catches the pair' — which is the general statement of the hole, not a fifth item. One consequence worth naming rather than fixing: T-004's checker now re-runs C-10's `eval-scope.sh` invocation and C-8's `--tier2-extract` run, on top of eleven judgment clauses across a document and four fixtures. That is the largest single check in the job and the likeliest place to see a `blocked`. It is the constitution's own check, so it is correct; it is just expensive.

PASS, change 3 closes. The missing conjunct is back in both places. The check_method names it among the four concrete instances ('whether any scenario or procedure step names a `tests/fixtures/` path as the run target'), and reaches it a second way through 'run each clause's check field in full', since it is C-10's own fourth sentence. The excerpt now carries the clause's both-halves form: 'Neither any scenario nor any step of the procedure may name a `tests/fixtures/` path as the directory the skill is run against' (constitution.md:74, 'No scenario, and no step of the procedure'). The split is now overlap rather than partition — T-001 takes the script half explicitly ('script half only; the run-procedure half belongs to T-004') and T-004 takes the whole clause — which is the right direction to err. Residual: the clause's per-run staging requirement lives in C-10's text ('It stages once per run, not once per scenario') and has no phase in C-10's own `check` field, so 'run the check field in full' does not reach it. It is reached anyway, but by the weaker route: T-004's 'The clause text is the contract' plus the excerpt's own statement of the rule at :53. Both workers are told correctly (T-001:43, T-004:53). Left as a residual because the constitution is settled and this is its gap, not the decomposition's, and because the decomposition did the one thing available to it — elevate the clause text over the check field.

PASS, change 4 closes. The graph is a DAG and the serialization is total: T-001 [] -> T-002 [T-001] -> T-005 [T-002] -> T-006 [T-005] -> T-003 [T-006] -> T-004 [all five]. No cycles, every referenced task exists, and the chain admits exactly one execution order, so no check can run against a tree another worker is writing into. That matters most for C-11, which is whole-repo and unqualified and is cited by all six tasks; under a total order every run of it sees a settled tree. C-1's whole-tree read is handled twice over — by the ordering, and by the sibling-tolerance note each task now carries. T-001's restatement is correct and correctly scoped: 'Sibling tasks in this job write into that same allowlist, so their files appearing in the diff is a pass, not a failure. What fails is a path outside it' — the inversion of the r0 sentence that would have failed T-001 for T-002's work. Two residuals. First, `deps` is a declaration; I can see no gate in this repo that enforces ordering at dispatch (the hooks live outside it), so the serialization is only as good as the dispatch discipline that honors it. Second, T-004's `deps: [T-001, T-002, T-003, T-005, T-006]` is redundant against the chain, but redundant-and-explicit is the right form for the one task that must open every artifact.

PASS, change 1 closes, and the clause coverage survived the cut whole. C-5 goes to T-002, C-6 to T-005, C-7 to T-006, and each of the three carries C-1, C-3 and C-11 alongside it exactly as the old combined task did — nothing was dropped in the split and nothing landed in two places. The behavior that r0 flagged as most likely to fall between them did not: the two-project client root travelled with the recurrence signal that needs it, into T-006 ('Build a client root with at least two project directories under it', plus 'If you use the recurrence signal ... the fixture has to actually hold those references, in distinct project directories, with the subject named in the notes there'). That re-derives correctly against scope-decisions.md:33-37, whose grep reads `<client-root>/{pursuits,projects}/*/notes/`, and against SKILL.md:35 for where a project sits. The interference finding is carried explicitly and in the right task: T-005's check requires 'that no `_inbox/` transcript names the positive slug's question aloud', with the reason attached ('the rule reads the transcript, not a designated file'), and the excerpt teaches it as 'The interference trap' rather than merely stating it. Cross-fixture interference is gone by construction now that each behavior owns a directory. Directory ownership is unambiguous in the sense that matters — each task owns exactly one directory and is told not to touch a sibling's — and identification runs through the worker's `artifacts` list, which is what '<the delivered directory>' in each check_method resolves against. Residual: no task fixes its directory name ('named for what it holds'), so a checker reading a tree with four sibling directories depends on that artifacts list to know which one is under test. Standard practice, and the serialization means the tree grows one directory at a time, but naming the directory in the task file would cost nothing.

findings.description: PASS, changes 6 and 7 close. All four drifted paraphrases are repaired against the clause text. C-2's locality rule is now stated as a ruling that pre-empts the precedent rather than as a restatement a worker could read past: 'The precedent states its fixtures once in a global `## Fixtures` block. You need that section too, but it does not satisfy C-2: every scenario must *also* name the fixture it runs against, inside its own section.' C-4's transplant test regains its qualifier verbatim in effect — 'would it stay true pasted into a different scenario, with or without its fixture name swapped? If so it has said nothing, and swapping in the right fixture name does not rescue it' — and the three named shapes are all back ('a token it omits, a section it invents, or a tier it picks instead'), where r0 found two. C-10 regains 'Neither any scenario nor any step of the procedure'. C-9's enumeration regains lint failure codes. The C-13 ruling is correct against the artifact, not merely plausible: `_maintenance/file-issue/EVALS.md` labels each scenario with standalone `**Prompt:**` and `**Repo:**` lines at :18-19, :33-34 and so on, which is not the bulleted `- **Thing:** description` form C-13 bans, and the ruling says exactly that. Three residuals, all decidable by a checker reading the clause. C-9's tightening on enumerated values ('`[tension: resolved|deferred|unacknowledged]` admits three, and nothing else') is still absent from the excerpt, and the tension scenario will write that token repeatedly; C-9's check field catches a wrong value, so this costs a rework round rather than shipping a defect. C-13's hard-wrap rule is still not in the excerpt, though it is the one item in that clause a checker decides by looking and an automatic fail — mitigated by the precedent being unwrapped and the excerpt telling the worker to match it. And the ruling settles the standalone label lines but not the precedent's `## Fixtures` bullets, which read `- **`fixture-bare`** — description`; that is the em-dash form, not the colon form the clause names, so a checker has a decidable rule either way.

PASS, re-derived across six tasks. Every acceptance criterion lands on a task that would produce or verify it, and every constitution clause is cited by at least one task. AC1 (fixture, prompt, pass condition per scenario) -> C-2, T-004. AC2 (with and without the skill, delta graded) -> C-4 per scenario and C-12's two-column results table, both T-004, with the second staged copy on T-001 and T-004. AC3 (contradiction round trip) -> C-5, T-002 fixture and T-004 document. AC4 (unacknowledged tension, own scenario) -> C-6, T-005 and T-004. AC5 (scope proposal across three tiers) -> C-7, T-006 and T-004, with the tiebreak as the fourth input. AC6 (nothing written to a real scope) -> C-10, T-001 script half and T-004 whole clause, plus C-11's shasum snapshot on all six. AC7 (doc beside the other maintainer evals) -> C-1 path and C-12 shape, T-004. The spec body's fourth behavior, 'whether generated summaries and entities are any good', -> C-8, T-003 and T-004. In the other direction: C-1 and C-11 on all six; C-3 on the four fixture tasks plus T-004; C-2, C-4, C-9, C-12 on T-004 alone, all correctly, being document-only clauses; C-13 on T-001 and T-004, which is exactly the scope its own text names ('`EVALS.md` and the comments in `eval-scope.sh`'). No spec requirement is uncovered and no clause is orphaned.

PASS, re-derived at the new task count. All six checkers are checker-judgment, and no task is a candidate for checker-deterministic: the routing table sends a clause checked by a rubric to checker-judgment, and every task carries at least two. T-001 remains the closest call and still fails the test — C-1 and C-11 are scripts, but C-10's script half requires judging the staged tree a faithful copy by diffing it, and C-13 is a comment audit. The three new fixture tasks each carry C-3 plus a behavior clause, both rubrics. T-004 carries eleven. Executors match the table by work rather than by default. worker-standard on sonnet for T-001 is a clear-spec shell script judged on correctness. worker-craft on opus for T-002, T-005 and T-006 is right, and stays right after the split: each one is a reading of SKILL.md:122 or scope-decisions.md where a wrong call produces a fixture that grades correct behavior as failure, which is judgment density rather than length — T-002 is now the smallest of the three and still belongs there for the amend-versus-supersede call. worker-standard on sonnet for T-003 sits on the boundary and remains defensible: the one trap is named explicitly in the excerpt and verification is mechanical. worker-craft on opus for T-004 is the user-facing taste artifact. Every `executor_model` matches its agent's tier in the table.

findings.description: PASS on all six. The r0 blocker was that one dispatch had to produce three unrelated behaviors and a FAIL on any clause reworked all of them under a mixed diagnosis; the split removes that outright, since each fixture task now maps one behavior to one clause to one directory, and a FAIL names one thing. T-001 is a single ~50-line shell script. T-002 is one accepted record, one contradicting input, optional decoys. T-005 needs two slugs across three or more prior notes each plus an acknowledging transcript, which lands near the size of the existing `mixed` fixture (six notes) and is comfortable for one opus dispatch. T-003 is a small v1 scope with one name and one fact planted below the `## Raw Content` fence. T-004 is one document, and its precedent is 109 lines. T-006 is the largest — a client root plus two opted-in project directories, each with `notes/` and `_memory/`, a `CLAUDE.md`, and four inbox inputs each validated against the full signal table — call it a dozen files. It is still one behavior, one clause and one coherent diagnosis on failure, so it stays inside one dispatch, but it is the one to watch if a retry budget starts burning.

PASS by relocation, with the fixture-side phrasing left as a residual. r0 failed this because both halves checked worker intent and the clause's own trap survived. The T-004 half is now fixed, and fixing it repairs the composition: T-004's checker runs C-8's check field in full, which opens with 'Run `--tier2-extract` against the fixture first ... Identify the note the scenario grades and confirm the run emitted that note's `<note-id>.extract.md`'. That is the clause's failing example caught at the only point where the graded note is known, since the scenario picking it does not exist until T-004. So the trap is closed and no bad artifact ships. What remains is a cost, not a hole: T-003's half still reads 'every note the fixture intends to grade' and 'confirm no gradable note is v2', and the fixture declares no intent, so a mixed fixture leaves T-003's checker guessing and pushes the real catch downstream into a late rework. The one-line repair r0 named still applies and is still free — every note under `<fixture>/notes/` is v1 and emits an extract, decidable from the fixture alone. Second residual, same task: the excerpt still never names `notes/` as where a gradable note has to sit, and migrate-scope.sh:319 only writes an extract from the non-record branch of `"$scope"/notes/*.md "$scope"/_memory/*/*.md "$scope"/entries/*.md`. Two things blunt it — the excerpt points at `old-only`, which has a `notes/` directory, and it requires the worker to run the extract themselves ('Verify by running the extract yourself') — so the silent-empty-scratch failure r0 described is now caught twice before a checker sees it. Naming the path would still be cheaper than either catch.

PASS, and r0's intent problem is closed by enumeration. T-006's half still opens in the language of intent ('the tier the input was built to elicit'), but the trailing clause makes it decidable from the artifact alone: 'project, client, journal, and one two-tier input resolving to the narrower token.' A checker does not need to know which input was meant to be which — it needs the four routings to come out as that set, which is exactly r0's proposed restatement. The non-textual signal is handled correctly on both sides: the check requires 'a second project directory exists and that its notes actually carry the subject', which matches scope-decisions.md:33-37's `grep -l -r "<subject>" "<client-root>"/{pursuits,projects}/*/notes/`, and the excerpt calls it out as 'the one signal in the table that is not readable off the input alone, and the one place a well-formed fixture can still grade nothing'. The doc-side pairing that nobody checked in r0 is now T-004's, unnarrowed. The tiebreak citation is accurate: scope-decisions.md:21-25 is the Conflict Resolution section, 'suggest the **narrowest** scope. Project is the floor.' Residual: 'its project subdirectories are themselves opted in where the tier requires it' leaves the checker to work out when the tier requires it. The answer is derivable — SKILL.md:30-35 walks up to the nearest directory holding `_inbox/` plus `_memory/`, so any project directory an input is groomed in must be opted in, while a project directory that exists only to hold the recurrence references needs `notes/` and nothing else — but the task says 'where the tier requires it' rather than saying that.

PASS on the split, subject to the blocker above. T-005's half carries both of the clause's load-bearing constraints intact — both slugs reach three or more files under `notes/`, so the negative case turns on acknowledgement and not on the count, and the negative acknowledgement sits in the `_inbox/` transcript under grooming — and both re-derive against the skill: the recurrence grep reads `<scope-root>/notes/` at SKILL.md:115 and 'Process mode never edits a prior note' at SKILL.md:124 is what forces the acknowledgement into the inbox. The interference check r0 asked for is present and correctly reasoned. The singular/plural question r0 raised is also settled, in the only place it could be: T-005 builds one directory carrying two slugs ('Own exactly one new directory', 'Two open-question slugs'), the check speaks of 'the negative slug' rather than r0's 'the negative fixture', and T-004 grades both branches 'in the same table', so C-2's singular 'the fixture it runs against' holds without strain. Residual: with the fixture holding two slugs, the number of `_inbox/` transcripts is load-bearing and unstated. Process mode grooms each inbox file, so if the worker plants two transcripts and only one names the negative question aloud, the negative outcome depends on which transcript the run is grooming. The check's 'the `_inbox/` transcript under grooming and nowhere else' reads as singular and a checker would likely catch a second transcript, but the excerpt never says one.

PASS on two of the three r0 shapes, and the third is the blocker above. No clause has both halves deferring to the other: C-3, C-5, C-6, C-7, C-8 and C-10 are each split with an explicit non-delegation sentence on the upstream side ('that half is not delegated back here', 'the run-procedure half belongs to T-004'), and the downstream side is T-004 running the whole clause check unnarrowed, which makes every split an overlap rather than a partition. Over-checking is the safe direction and it is the direction taken. On checks that assume work nobody performs, the instrument checks resolve: T-004's C-10 phase needs `eval-scope.sh`, delivered by T-001 upstream in the chain; its C-8 phase needs a fixture that emits extracts, delivered by T-003; its C-12 phase needs `_maintenance/file-issue/EVALS.md`, which exists; C-2's terminal-boundary check needs a `## Grading` heading and numbered scenario sections, both required by T-004's excerpt. The one check that assumes something nobody performs is the fixture lint, recorded as the blocker. On excerpts that would have a worker guess, the r0 instances are closed — the C-13 precedent collision is ruled, the C-2 locality rule is stated, T-001's `grep -q` contradiction is resolved by repointing the house-style reference at `verify-migration.sh`, which contains zero uses of it where `migrate-scope.sh` has two — and what is left is residual: T-003's unnamed `notes/`, T-004's unstated hard-wrap rule, T-005's unstated transcript count. Against those sits one excerpt statement that is not a guess but a false fact, which is why the lint finding is a blocker rather than a residual: a worker told 'a malformed one is a lint failure' has been told not to check by hand.
